title: Scaring Our Children To Death
author: Peter Greene
summary: Greene responds to alarming reports of a youth mental health crisis by pointing at one factor, an adult culture and politics of constant fear and anger. He argues that adults can treat the endless apocalyptic rhetoric as background noise, but students have lived inside it their entire lives. Schools sit downhill from that culture, and the messages sent to students about their fragility, whether protective bubbles or the armour of grit, compound the harm. He calls on adults to affirm young people as strong and resilient and to stop leading with doom. It is an opinion piece with limited evidence but a clear thesis about the climate students inhabit.
points: The author singles out the political strategy of whipping up fear and anger as a driver of student anxiety, beyond the pandemic and social media.
Students born into a culture already screaming Fire have never known anything else, so what is background noise to adults defines their world.
The messages schools send about student weakness, protective bubbles or compensatory grit, reinforce a sense of fragility.
Young people are described as canaries in a cultural coal mine, and adults are urged to affirm their strength and resilience.
The cultural message has lost the idea that things may be hard but we are tough enough to get through them.
quotes: This alarm has been rung again and again over the past year, including a declaration of a national emergency in the fall of 2021 from the American Academy of Pediatrics (and underlined it this year), but for folks working in the field, it's not exactly news. I wrote about this, sort of, in 2015, and did so in response to a story about the high rate of teen suicides in Silicon Valley. Back then I focused on the One Wrong Move syndrome, the message we send students that a single screw-up, a critical failure, can leave your whole life in shambles.

But we live in different times. For the past couple of decades, the go-to political strategy is to whip up fear and anger, anger and fear. From the days when every initiative was The War On [Your Cause Here], we have moved on to an endless series of existential crises. Every election is about the continued existence of democracy and/or our country. Every Congress vote is critical test; every Supreme Court decision is a turning point in the struggle for our very existence.

But if you're a young person in this country, you were born into a theater where people were already screaming "Fire," and your whole life, they have never stopped. Our constant soup of rage and fear may be background noise to adults, but to students, it defines the world they have navigated for their entire lives.

For students, in addition to the general noise about onrushing catastrophe, we send messages about their weakness, about all the things they must be protected from because otherwise they'll be broken and bent, about how they must either be kept in a protective bubble or taught to put on the armor of "grit" or some other quality that we imply they naturally lack.

I expect that plenty of people will not heed any of this, that the plight of the canaries will not move them. We are a culture that likes to talk about how we value children, especially when we're using it to justify our latest policy initiative, but our actions and choices show that mostly we aren't serious about it. But we could be. We could decide tomorrow to do better
